subtitle: Selective Focus, Blindness, Contemplation, and the Architecture of Notice

chapters.title: The Fifty-Bit Bottleneck
chapters.subtitle: Cocktail Parties, Dichotic Tapes, and Why the Conscious Mind Can Only Hear One Voice at a Time
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1953 at Imperial College London, Colin Cherry built a dichotic tape-shadowing apparatus to isolate the cocktail party problem, followed by Donald Broadbent's 1958 Cambridge split-ear air-traffic control filter model and Anne Treisman's 1960 Oxford speech-switching experiments.
chapters.exit_fact: When Anne Treisman swapped two prose passages mid-sentence between her Oxford listeners' left and right headphones in 1960, subjects unconsciously jumped to the ignored ear for one or two words to keep the sentence grammatical before snapping back to their assigned channel.

chapters.title: The Two-Degree Keyhole
chapters.subtitle: Alfred Yarbus, Suction-Cup Mirrors, and Why You Are Blind for Forty Minutes Every Day
chapters.historical_anchor: Building on Émile Javal's 1879 Paris discovery of ballistic eye saccades, Alfred Yarbus in 1965 at Moscow's Institute for Information Transmission Problems attached mirrored rubber suction caps directly to anesthetized human corneas to record scanpaths across Ilya Repin's painting An Unexpected Visitor.
chapters.exit_fact: Because a human executes roughly 150,000 ballistic saccades across sixteen waking hours—each lasting thirty to fifty milliseconds while corollary discharge silences motion processing—the brain actively shuts down visual motion for more than forty minutes every day without the observer noticing a gap.

chapters.title: Looked But Failed to See
chapters.subtitle: Runway Collisions, Invisible Gorillas, and the Illusion of a Complete Visual Field
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1980 at NASA Ames Research Center, Richard Haines and Edith Fischer tested commercial airline captains in a Boeing 727 simulator equipped with windshield head-up displays, anticipating Arien Mack and Irvin Rock's 1998 psychophysical trials and Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris's 1999 Harvard basketball-pass gorilla study.
chapters.exit_fact: When Daniel Memmert repeated the basketball-pass study using infrared corneal eye trackers, the observers who swore no gorilla had entered the room had fixated their foveas directly on the gorilla's chest for an average of one full second—the exact same fixation count as those who spotted her immediately.

chapters.title: The Spotlight and the Floodlight
chapters.subtitle: Milanese Cathedrals, Hemispheric Asymmetry, and the Two Ways a Brain Attends to the World
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1978 at the University of Milan, Edoardo Bisiach and Claudio Luzzatti tested right-parietal stroke patients describing the Piazza del Duomo from two opposite mental viewpoints, illuminating Lesley Rogers's 1979 avian lateralization findings, Marek Marsel Mesulam's 1981 spatial asymmetry model, and Iain McGilchrist's synthesis of divided hemispheric attention.
chapters.exit_fact: When Bisiach and Luzzatti asked patient I.G. to imagine walking across the Piazza del Duomo and turning around to face the cathedral doors, the northern palaces that had vanished from his memory sixty seconds earlier when they sat on his imagined left reappeared in crisp detail once they shifted to his imagined right.

chapters.title: The Mismatch Alarm
chapters.subtitle: Pavlov's Interrupted Dogs, Silent Tones, and the Mathematics of Surprise
chapters.historical_anchor: After Ivan Pavlov observed around 1910 in St. Petersburg that a stranger's footsteps instantly froze conditioned salivation via the orienting reflex, Evgeny Sokolov in 1960 at Moscow State University proved that a quieter or omitted tone triggers the same autonomic alarm, formalized in 2005 by Laurent Itti and Pierre Baldi as Kullback-Leibler Bayesian surprise.
chapters.exit_fact: In Sokolov's Moscow chamber, repeating a sixty-decibel tone twenty times extinguished the subject's orienting response completely, yet dropping the twenty-first tone to forty decibels—or omitting it on schedule—triggered an immediate skin-conductance spike because the quiet violated the cortex's timing template.

chapters.title: The Myth of Multitasking
chapters.subtitle: Refractory Bottlenecks, Hands-Free Crashes, and the Cost of Attention Residue
chapters.historical_anchor: Building on Harold Pashler's 1994 UC San Diego proof of the serial Psychological Refractory Period bottleneck, David Strayer and William Johnston at the University of Utah demonstrated in 2001–2006 that hands-free cell-phone conversations impair driving more than a 0.08 percent blood alcohol level, while Sophie Leroy in 2009 identified attention residue across task switches.
chapters.exit_fact: When Strayer's team recorded P300 event-related brain potentials while drivers stared directly at braking lead vehicles during a hands-free phone conversation, the amplitude of the parietal P300 wave dropped by fifty percent, proving that spoken conversation starves visual encoding at the central bottleneck even when both hands are on the wheel.

chapters.title: The Watchman's Trap
chapters.subtitle: Royal Air Force Radar Scopes, Signal Detection, and Why Vigilance Collapses in the Quiet
chapters.historical_anchor: In November 1943 at Cambridge, Norman Mackworth built his jumping Clock Test for Royal Air Force Coastal Command to explain why airborne radar operators missed surfaced German U-boats after thirty minutes on patrol, laying the empirical foundation for David Green and John Swets's 1966 Signal Detection Theory and Jeremy Wolfe's 2005 low-prevalence effect.
chapters.exit_fact: In Jeremy Wolfe's 2005 baggage-screening trials at Harvard Medical School, dropping weapon prevalence from fifty percent of X-ray bags down to one percent caused trained observers to shift their decision criterion so conservatively that their miss rate more than quadrupled from seven percent to thirty percent.

chapters.title: The Magical Number Four
chapters.subtitle: George Miller, Nelson Cowan, and Why Working Memory Is Controlled Attention
chapters.historical_anchor: After George Miller's 1956 Harvard paper distinguished seven-item chunked memory span from single-dimension channel capacity, Nelson Cowan in 2001 demonstrated a strict three-to-four-slot limit when rehearsal is blocked, and Randall Engle at Georgia Tech proved that working-memory capacity reflects executive attention's power to block distraction.
chapters.exit_fact: In Edward Vogel, Machizawa, and Steven Luck's 2005 electrophysiological trials, individuals with low working-memory scores showed just as much parietal neural activity as high-capacity observers—not because they held more targets, but because their executive gate failed and let irrelevant background distractors flood their four slots.

chapters.title: The Slot Machine in the Pocket
chapters.subtitle: Skinner's Pigeons, Dopamine Prediction Errors, and the Engineering of Compulsion
chapters.historical_anchor: Starting with B. F. Skinner and Charles Ferster's 1957 Harvard variable-ratio pigeon schedules, Wolfram Schultz demonstrated in the 1990s that primate midbrain dopamine neurons code reward prediction errors rather than pleasure itself, while Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson dissociated dopaminergic wanting from hedonic liking.
chapters.exit_fact: When Wolfram Schultz delivered a drop of fruit juice on a fifty-percent uncertain schedule after a visual cue, tonic midbrain dopamine ramping climbed to its absolute maximum during the delay before the outcome arrived, proving that maximal uncertainty—not guaranteed reward—drives the strongest neurochemical pull on attention.

chapters.title: The Wandering Mind
chapters.subtitle: Experience Sampling, the Default Mode Network, and the Hidden Work of Daydreaming
chapters.historical_anchor: In 2001 at Washington University in St. Louis, Marcus Raichle discovered via oxygen-15 PET scans that the midline Default Mode Network burns maximal energy at rest, followed by Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert's 2010 Harvard iPhone study of 2,250 adults and Jonathan Schooler and Benjamin Baird's 2012 creative-incubation trials.
chapters.exit_fact: across 250,000 real-time smartphone samples collected by Killingsworth and Gilbert in 2010, human minds wandered away from their current activity during 46.9 percent of waking hours, and never dropped below thirty percent off-task during any single human activity except making love.

chapters.title: The Sovereign Faculty
chapters.subtitle: William James, Simone Weil, and the Moral Weight of Patient Notice
chapters.historical_anchor: In his 1890 treatise The Principles of Psychology at Harvard, William James defined the repeated act of retrieving a wandering attention as the root of judgment, character, and will, a phenomenological insight transformed in the mid-twentieth century by French philosopher Simone Weil and Oxford moral philosopher Iris Murdoch.
chapters.exit_fact: In 2008, Heleen Slagter and Richard Davidson's electrophysiological recordings of practitioners trained in non-grasping open-monitoring contemplation showed that reducing the emotional and attentional over-investment in a first visual target nearly eliminated the half-second attentional blink that normally blinds observers to a second target.

chapters.title: From Selective Filter to All-to-All Weights
chapters.subtitle: How Transformers Replaced Sequential Memory With Scaled Dot-Product Attention
chapters.historical_anchor: To overcome the fixed-vector bottleneck that caused recurrent neural networks to forget the beginning of long sentences, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio in Montreal introduced neural alignment in 2014, culminating in Ashish Vaswani and seven Google colleagues' June 2017 Transformer architecture.
chapters.exit_fact: By discarding recurrent step-by-step memory altogether and computing scaled dot-product compatibility scores between every pair of tokens in parallel, the 2017 Transformer turned attention from a biological survival filter that throws away 99.999 percent of experience into a differentiable all-to-all routing matrix.
